title: RFQ Meaning, Types and Process: How RFQs Work
summary: RFQ stands for request for quotation. Learn the RFQ process step by step, the RFQ workflow stages, what it means across industries, and how vendors should respond.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


- RFQ stands for request for quotation, sometimes written request for quote. It is a document a buyer sends to vendors asking for pricing and delivery terms on a clearly defined product or service.
- The RFQ workflow covers the operational stages a quote request moves through internally, while the RFQ process describes the wider buyer and vendor transaction around it.
- The RFQ process runs through six stages: the buyer issues it, vendors qualify and decide whether to bid, vendors prepare and submit quotes, the buyer evaluates, an award is issued, and a purchase order or contract follows.
- There are four common RFQ formats: open, invited, sealed, and reverse auction. Each changes what vendors can see and how pricing should be set.
- A submitted quote is generally a firm offer that becomes binding once the buyer accepts it, which is why unstated assumptions in a quote create real exposure.
- Turnaround is short, often 24 to 72 hours for commercial RFQs, so a fast internal qualification step matters more than a polished document.
- What an RFQ means shifts by industry. In manufacturing it is a build-to-print pricing request, in sales it is an inbound buying signal, and in trading it is an electronic protocol for requesting executable quotes.
- Vendors lose RFQs on administrative grounds more often than on price: wrong format, missing documentation, or a missed deadline.


RFQs are transactional, time-sensitive, and usually decided on a narrow set of commercial criteria. That makes them very different from RFPs, where strategy and methodology carry the evaluation.


This guide covers how the RFQ process works from both sides, what happens at each stage, the four RFQ formats you will encounter, and where vendors most often lose quotes they should have won.


## What is a request for quote (RFQ)?


RFQ stands for request for quotation, also written as request for quote. It is a document a buyer sends to vendors asking for pricing and delivery terms on a specific, well-defined product or service.


The buyer already knows what they need, so an RFQ asks what it costs and how fast it can be delivered rather than how the problem should be solved. That is the core distinction from an RFP, which asks vendors to propose an approach.


Because the specification is fixed, evaluation is largely quantitative. Price, lead time, and compliance with stated terms drive the decision, with vendor qualification acting as a threshold rather than a scored differentiator in most commercial RFQs.


RFQs are common for commoditized goods, hardware, raw materials, logistics, printing, and standardized services. They also appear late in a longer procurement cycle, after an RFI has mapped the market and an RFP has settled the approach.


The core distinction against the other two documents is short. An RFI asks who can do this, an RFP asks how you would do it, and an RFQ asks what it costs. Where you need the full breakdown, the[differences between RFI, RFP, and RFQ](https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/rfi-rfp-meaning) and the[direct RFQ and RFP comparison](https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/differences-rfq-rfp) both go deeper than is useful here.


## What RFQ means in different industries


The abbreviation is consistent but the practice behind it varies, and a vendor reading an RFQ from an unfamiliar sector often misjudges what is expected.


Context What an RFQ means there What the requester expects back


Procurement A formal solicitation for pricing against a fixed specification Itemized pricing, lead time, payment terms


Manufacturing A build-to-print request, usually with drawings, tolerances, and volumes attached Unit price at stated quantities, tooling cost, lead time, capability confirmation


Sales An inbound buying signal from a prospect who has defined their requirement A fast, accurate quote, since response speed materially affects win rate here


Construction A subcontractor or supplier pricing request against a scope package Trade pricing, inclusions and exclusions, schedule availability


Logistics and supply chain A rate request for defined lanes, volumes, or service levels Rate per lane or unit, accessorial charges, capacity commitment


Financial trading An electronic protocol where a participant requests executable quotes from selected dealers A firm, time-limited two-way price


Two of these are worth separating out. In manufacturing, an RFQ frequently arrives as a technical package rather than a document, and quoting requires engineering review before pricing, which is why manufacturing RFQ turnaround is measured in days rather than hours.


In financial trading, RFQ is not a procurement document at all. It is an execution mechanism used in fixed income, derivatives, and increasingly crypto markets, where a participant requests quotes from a chosen set of liquidity providers rather than trading on a public order book. If you arrived here looking for that meaning, the rest of this guide covers the procurement sense of the term.


## The 4 types of RFQ


RFQs come in four formats, and which one you are responding to changes how much information you have and how aggressively you should price.


- **Open RFQ:** Published publicly so any qualified supplier can respond, common in public-sector procurement. Vendor identities and sometimes bid values become visible, which makes pricing more competitive and margins thinner.
- **Invited RFQ:** Sent to a pre-qualified shortlist, typical in commercial procurement where the buyer has an approved supplier list. The field is smaller and past performance carries weight alongside price.
- **Sealed RFQ:** Quotes are submitted confidentially and opened simultaneously at a set time, so no vendor can adjust against another. Standard in government contracting and any process where the award must be demonstrably fair.
- **Reverse auction RFQ:** Vendors bid in real time against each other, with the price visible and declining through the session. Used for commoditized categories with high volume, and it compresses margin by design.


Two consequences follow for vendors. In a sealed or open process, your first submission is your only one, so there is no room to hold back on price expecting a second round. In a reverse auction, set a walk-away floor before the session starts, since the format is built to push bidding below the point where the work is worth taking.


## How the RFQ process works, step by step


The RFQ process moves through six stages from issue to purchase order. Timelines are short compared with RFPs, often days rather than weeks.


### Stage 1: The buyer defines requirements and issues the RFQ


The buyer specifies the product or service, quantity, delivery timeline, pricing format, payment terms, evaluation criteria, and submission instructions. Precision here determines quote quality, since vendors pricing against a vague specification will either pad for uncertainty or quote against assumptions the buyer never intended.


The RFQ goes out to a vetted supplier list or onto a procurement platform, with identical information and deadlines for every recipient.


### Stage 2: Vendors qualify the opportunity


Vendors assess fit before committing effort, checking scope alignment, margin viability, delivery capacity, and whether they hold any real advantage. With 24 to 72 hour deadlines common, a slow internal qualification step consumes the time needed to price properly.


The practical filter is whether you can meet the specification as written at a price you would be willing to deliver at. If either half fails, responding costs you time and signals nothing useful to the buyer.


### Stage 3: Vendors prepare and submit quotes


The quote covers unit pricing, total cost, lead time, payment terms, validity period, and any documentation the RFQ requires. Coordination across sales, pricing, operations, and occasionally legal happens inside a compressed window.


State assumptions explicitly. A quote that depends on a minimum order quantity, a specific delivery location, or current material pricing should say so, because an assumption you leave unstated becomes a commitment you are held to.


### Stage 4: The buyer evaluates quotes


The buyer compares submissions against the criteria published in the RFQ, usually price first, then lead time, then compliance with stated terms and vendor qualification. Clarification requests may go out where a quote is ambiguous or incomplete.


Non-compliant quotes are frequently set aside before evaluation begins rather than scored down, which is why format and completeness matter as much as the number.


### Stage 5: Award and notification


The buyer selects a vendor and notifies them, usually informing unsuccessful vendors at the same time. Open and sealed public processes often publish the award and the winning value.


Feedback is not automatic in commercial RFQs, but it is usually available on request and is the cheapest competitive intelligence you will get.


### Stage 6: Purchase order or contract


The award converts into a purchase order or a supply contract, which is the document that actually binds both parties. Terms from the accepted quote typically carry directly into it, so anything you did not want to commit to should not have been in the quote.


## The RFQ workflow inside a vendor team


The RFQ workflow is the internal sequence a quote request moves through once it arrives, as distinct from the buyer-side process around it. Teams handling volume need this mapped explicitly, because most delay is internal rather than external.


A typical vendor-side workflow has six stages:


- **Intake and logging:** The request arrives by email, portal, or EDI and is recorded with its deadline, source, and requirement summary. Requests that sit in an individual inbox rather than a shared queue are where most missed deadlines originate.
- **Qualification:** A go or no-go decision against scope fit, margin, and capacity, ideally within the first few hours rather than the first day.
- **Technical review:** Engineering, operations, or delivery confirms the requirement can be met as specified and flags any deviation. In manufacturing this stage dominates the timeline.
- **Costing:** Input costs, labor, and any subcontract or freight elements are assembled into a cost basis.
- **Pricing and approval:** Margin is applied and the quote is approved at whatever authority level the value requires. Unclear approval thresholds are the single most common internal bottleneck.
- **Submission and logging:** The quote goes out in the required format, and both the quote and its assumptions are recorded for follow-up and win/loss analysis.


Mapping this once, with named owners and target durations per stage, tends to surface the bottleneck immediately. In most teams it is either qualification, because nobody owns the decision, or pricing approval, because the authority matrix is undefined.


## How to prioritize RFQs when you are short on time


When volume exceeds capacity, prioritize on expected value rather than arrival order or deadline proximity. Deadline-driven triage systematically favors whichever request happens to be most urgent, not whichever is most winnable.


Rank incoming requests against four factors:


- **Win probability:** Incumbency, prior relationship, and whether the specification appears written around a competitor's product.
- **Contract value and margin:** Annualized value where the requirement repeats, not just the single order.
- **Strategic value:** Whether the account opens a category, geography, or reference you want.
- **Cost to quote:** Requests needing engineering review or custom costing consume disproportionate internal capacity.


The practical rule is that a high-value request you are unlikely to win deserves less attention than a moderate-value request you are well positioned for. Declining explicitly is also better than submitting a rushed quote, since buyers remember both, and a polite decline preserves the relationship for the next request.


## Is an RFQ legally binding?


An RFQ itself does not bind the buyer to purchase, but a submitted quote is generally treated as a firm offer, and acceptance by the buyer can form a contract.


This is the asymmetry vendors most often misjudge. The buyer retains the right to reject all quotes, cancel the process, or award to none. The vendor, having submitted a priced offer against a defined specification, is usually bound by it once the buyer accepts within the validity period.


Three practices follow from that:


- **Set a validity period explicitly:** A quote stating that pricing holds for 30 days protects you against acceptance six months later at costs that no longer apply.
- **Write assumptions into the quote itself:** Pricing based on a minimum quantity, a stated delivery point, or current input costs needs to be recorded in the document, not discussed verbally.
- **Check the buyer's terms before quoting:** Public-sector RFQs in particular often state that submission constitutes acceptance of the buyer's standard terms, which may include liability or penalty clauses you would otherwise negotiate.


Rules vary by jurisdiction and by whether the buyer is a public body, so treat this as the general position rather than legal advice on a specific solicitation.


## What buyers include in an RFQ


Most RFQs contain seven elements, and vendors should confirm each one is addressed before submitting.


- **Product or service description:** The technical specification, materials, features, or service requirements defining exactly what is being purchased.
- **Quantity or volume:** Units, licenses, or service hours required, including any tiering that affects unit pricing.
- **Delivery timeline:** Required delivery date or project window, sometimes with milestone dates for phased supply.
- **Pricing format:** How costs must be presented, whether per unit, per hour, or bundled, often with a template to complete.
- **Payment terms:** When and how payment occurs, such as net-30, on delivery, or staged against milestones.
- **Evaluation criteria:** What the buyer weighs, typically price, lead time, and qualification, with weighting where it is published.
- **Submission instructions:** Deadline, format, delivery channel, required attachments, and the contact for clarifications.


Follow the instructions exactly. A missing document or the wrong file format disqualifies a competitive quote before anyone reads the pricing.


## Why vendors lose RFQs


Most lost quotes fail on execution rather than price. The recurring causes:


- **Missing the deadline or the format:** Late submissions and wrong file types are treated as non-responsive in most procurement processes, with no discretion applied.
- **Quoting against assumptions that were never stated:** When the buyer's understanding and yours differ, the gap surfaces after award and costs either margin or the relationship.
- **Incomplete documentation:** Omitted certifications, insurance evidence, or required forms remove otherwise strong quotes from consideration.
- **Pricing without checking input costs:** Quotes built on stale material or labor costs win the award and lose money, particularly on long validity periods.
- **Responding to everything:** Teams without a qualification filter spread effort across low-fit opportunities and submit weaker quotes on the ones they could have won.
- **Ignoring the clarification window:** Ambiguities in the specification can be resolved before submission, and buyers usually share answers with all bidders, so the question costs nothing.
- **No win/loss tracking:** Without recording outcomes and reasons, pricing strategy never improves across cycles.

## How to respond to RFQs faster


Speed matters disproportionately in RFQ processes because the evaluation window is short and buyers are comparing near-identical offerings. Four changes have the most effect:


- **Qualify in under an hour:** A fixed go/no-go checklist covering scope fit, margin, capacity, and competitive position removes the internal debate that consumes the first day.
- **Maintain a reusable content library:** Standard service descriptions, terms, certifications, and pricing frameworks should be assembled rather than rewritten for each quote.
- **Pre-agree pricing authority:** Knowing in advance who can approve what discount, and within what range, prevents quotes stalling in internal approval on day two.
- **Track outcomes systematically:** Recording what won, what lost, and at what price turns each cycle into pricing intelligence rather than a one-off transaction.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### How long do buyers give vendors to respond to an RFQ?


Commercial RFQs commonly allow 24 to 72 hours for straightforward commoditized items, extending to one or two weeks where the specification is technical or requires subcontractor pricing. Public-sector RFQs usually allow longer, often two to four weeks, because procurement regulations set minimum notice periods.


### How do I know if an RFQ is worth responding to?


Check four things: whether the scope matches what you actually supply, whether the volume and price point clear your margin threshold, whether you have delivery capacity in the required window, and whether you hold any advantage on price, lead time, or incumbency. If none of the four is a clear yes, the effort is better spent elsewhere.


### What should I do when an RFQ lacks enough detail to price accurately?


Use the clarification window if one exists, since answers are usually circulated to all bidders and the question costs nothing. Where no clarification is possible, state your assumptions explicitly in the quote rather than guessing silently. A quote with documented assumptions is defensible, while one without them transfers all the risk to you.


### Can I negotiate after submitting a quote?


Sometimes, but do not price expecting to. Invited and repeat-vendor RFQs occasionally allow a revision round, usually buyer-initiated. Sealed and open public processes generally do not, since post-submission negotiation would undermine the fairness the format exists to protect. Submit your realistic best price the first time.


### What is a reverse auction and should I participate?


A reverse auction is a live bidding session where vendors compete on visible, declining price. It suits high-volume commoditized supply and compresses margin deliberately. Participate only with a predetermined floor, and only where you have a genuine cost advantage, since the format rewards low cost structure rather than differentiation.


### What happens between the award and the purchase order?


The buyer converts the accepted quote into a purchase order or supply contract, usually carrying the quoted terms directly across. Review what arrives against what you quoted before accepting, since terms occasionally shift during conversion, and the purchase order rather than your quote is what governs delivery.


### Do RFQs always go to the lowest price?


Not always, though price dominates more than in RFP evaluations. Lead time, compliance with stated terms, quality history, and supply reliability all factor in, and public buyers in particular often evaluate on lowest responsive and responsible bid, which means the cheapest quote that also meets every stated requirement and comes from a qualified supplier.


### Can we revise a quote after submitting it?


It depends on the format and whether the deadline has passed. Before the deadline, most buyers accept a revised submission that clearly supersedes the original, though you should state plainly that it replaces the earlier version. After the deadline, sealed and open public processes generally do not permit revision, since that would undermine the fairness the format protects. Commercial and invited RFQs are more flexible, and a buyer-initiated clarification round sometimes allows correction. Where you spot a material error after submitting, raise it immediately rather than waiting, since a withdrawn quote is recoverable and an accepted quote priced wrongly is not.


### How do we reduce RFQ response time without losing accuracy?


Attack the internal stages rather than the drafting. In most teams the delay sits in qualification, where nobody owns the decision, and in pricing approval, where authority thresholds are undefined. Fixing those two removes more elapsed time than faster writing ever will. Beyond that, a maintained library of standard terms, capability statements, and cost templates means each quote assembles rather than starts blank.


### What information should a vendor include when responding to an RFQ?


Unit and total pricing in the format requested, lead time, validity period, payment terms, any documentation the RFQ specifies, and your assumptions stated explicitly. Include exactly what was asked for and nothing that contradicts it. Additional marketing material rarely helps in an RFQ evaluation and occasionally hurts, since it signals you have not understood that the decision is commercial rather than persuasive.


### Should I quote if I cannot meet one requirement?


It depends on whether the requirement is mandatory or preferred. Mandatory requirements are pass or fail, and a non-compliant quote is usually set aside without scoring. Where a requirement is preferred, quoting with a clearly noted exception and an alternative can still compete, provided the deviation is stated rather than hidden.
